item.title: Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs on US as high as 50%
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3v4xg5klx7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs on US as high as 50% - Published Canada has announced counter-tariffs as high as 50% on a range of US goods in retaliation to the latest wave of levies on Canadian imports imposed by President Donald Trump last weekend. The Canadian tariffs will apply to nearly C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) worth of American products, ranging from steel to furniture, fresh tuna and cotton T-shirts, officials announced on Tuesday. The list of targeted products is designed to match Canadian goods hit by the US. The Canadian levies are set to come into effect on 8 September. It is the latest escalation after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making last-minute demands that were unreasonable. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said that Canada's retaliation is in response to 50% tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on a range of Canadian goods after trade talks fell apart on Friday. "Those tariffs will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses and communities across our nation," he said. "Canada must respond." Champagne characterised Canada's retaliation as "proportionate" and "strategic". He added that Canada will also offer businesses and workers impacted by US tariffs an additional C$7.5bn for support programmes designed to minimise job losses and keep companies afloat. Placing taxes on trade between what are historically two of the world's closest trading partners will undoubtedly lead to pain on both sides of the border. Supply chains which have been developed over decades are set to see increased trading costs due the latest tariff announcements made from both the US and Canada, ultimately hitting businesses of all sizes and consumers through potentially higher prices. Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support their government in holding firm against the US. But some questions remain on exactly why trade talks fell apart, with the Conservative opposition asking that the full text of the draft deal with the US be released. Businesses have also expressed concerns about the impact of a prolonged trade war with Canada's largest trading partner. The White House released a statement after Canada announced its counter-tariffs, saying that the US was prepared to offer Canada "the most preferential market access of any country on Earth" in recent trade talks. "Instead of partnership, Canada chose unreasonable demands, walk-backs, and flat-out rejection," it said. In a series of Tuesday posts on Truth Social, Trump also accused Canada of "ripping off" the US for decades and of charging American farmers steep tariffs. "I deal with many countries, and Canada is easily the most difficult and unreasonable," Trump wrote. "They feel entitled, but they are not a State, and will be entitled no longer!" He suggested that he will change the name of Lake Ontario, one of the Great Lakes on the US-Canada border, to Lake America, writing: "We don't expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer." Trump threatened this week to hike US tariffs on Canadian automobiles to 50% as of 1 January. Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by accusing Trump of wanting to "destroy" Canadian industries including the automobile manufacturing and steel and aluminum sectors. Public rhetoric on both sides reached a fever pitch on Monday, but some officials struck a more diplomatic tone on Tuesday with hopes that talks could be resumed. After calling Trump a "loser" on Monday at a news conference, Ontario Premier Doug Ford acknowledged in an interview with CNN that "things got a little heated". "But I want to make a deal — a good deal for the American people, a good deal for Canadians," Ford said. The escalation also puts into question the future of a North American free trade pact between Canada, the US and Mexico called the USMCA. President Claudia Sheinbaum had despatched her economy secretary, Marcelo Ebrard, to Washington for emergency talks after trade negotiations collapsed with Canada. - How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump - Published1 day ago - 'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war - Published1 day ago Which US goods will be hit by tariffs? Canada released on Tuesday a list of nearly 900 US products that will be hit by its counter-tariffs. The list includes: - A 50% tariff on steel and aluminum products that were previously only subject to a 25% counter tariff - A 50% tariff on various other goods including natural honey, furniture, clothing and apparel, makeup and perfume - A 25% tariff on goods including appliances, like dishwashers and washing machines, dairy products, such as cheese, fish and seafood, and certain steel and aluminum derivative products - A 15% tariff on certain types of tools and machinery, including forklifts and air conditioning machines Canadian officials said they chose products that consumers and businesses in Canada could source elsewhere in an attempt to minimise hurt at home.

item.title: China hits out at 'illegal' new US sanctions on Iran and trading partners
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyl8965j5go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
China hits out at 'illegal' new US sanctions on Iran and trading partners - Published China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include Beijing. Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights. This came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Monday, warning any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated. China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, although the trade has declined under the US blockade of Iran's ports. Lin said: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted." Bessent described the plans for sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, warning banks and businesses would share in Iran's isolation if they refused to cut ties with the country. He declined to focus on specific nations, but said US President Donald Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime". However, responding to a question about Chinese banks, Bessent said he wanted to make clear "no one was above the reach of US sanctions". The announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month. Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products. Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US. China's response followed Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh saying Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he said would lead to "another defeat" for the US. "The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television. "We also have our own tools and know how to play the game," he said, adding Tehran had been "waiting for these plans for a long time". - Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions - Published22 hours ago The US has dubbed its latest sanctions "Operation Economic Outcast" and described them as an "economic D-Day" against Iran. It comes almost six months after the start of the Iran war. The conflict has since led to hikes in oil prices worldwide, with Tehran effectively blocking exports through the Strait of Hormuz - a waterway vital to the global economy. The US has also slowed traffic via its own naval blockade. Recent attempts to end the conflict via diplomacy have failed, and a 60-day ceasefire formally expired last week with no sign of a settlement. With the announcement of new sanctions, the US treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it". UK Chancellor John Healey said the British government supported "US work to secure a diplomatic solution and welcome efforts to increase pressure". Iran is already under heavy sanctions from the US, but Bessent said these go further. He said the Treasury had mapped financial channels, facilitators and networks used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil, imposing sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels. But analysts had cast doubt on the latest measures even before China's response. David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told the BBC the direct impact on Iran's energy revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib". "We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term," he added. This is partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, he said, "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either". Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group, said: "Generally, the Chinese are against unilateral sanctions. They would comply with multilateral or international sanctions, but unilateral sanctions just imposed by the US - they have always seen that as illegitimate." And although Iran's neighbours like Pakistan, Turkey and Iraq want to maintain good relationships with the US, they "can't really afford to cut off ties with Iran", Vaez told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. He said putting economic pressure on Tehran "doesn't work" because the Iranian regime is willing to "absorb any pain" and pass it onto the people. Other trade partners that could be affected by the US announcement include India and Russia, who have not yet responded.

item.title: CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c87vg9x5d7do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports - Published The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported. John Ratcliffe reportedly arrived in the Russian capital earlier on Tuesday. Neither Washington or Moscow have confirmed the nature of the visit or who he was due to meet. In-person talks between high-level American and Russian officials are rare. Flight tracking data confirmed a large US military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday. It departed later on Tuesday. BBC News has contacted the CIA, the White House and Pentagon for comment. Footage posted on social media showed the C-17 transport plane approaching Moscow's Vnukovo international airport. It departed Riga airport at 05:50 GMT and appeared to have landed in the Russian capital at around 07:04 GMT, according to data from FlightRadar24. It returned to Riga shortly before 17:00 GMT. Footage on social media also purported to show a diplomatic motorcade travelling through Moscow. Ahead of the trip, the US told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to suspend strikes until they had left, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS. The trip is thought to be Ratcliffe's first trip to Russia as CIA director, although he has maintained contact with his intelligence counterparts in Moscow. John Foreman, who served as a British military attaché to Moscow between 2019 and 2022, told Radio 4's PM programme that the visit could be focused on "escalation management" given speculation recent drone activity in Germany could be linked to Russia. He said: "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up." Foreman said the trip could also concern the release of US detainees currently being held in Russia. Ratcliffe played a role in negotiations for the release of Russian-American citizen Ksenia Karelina, who was jailed in Russia for over a year after being accused of providing support to Ukraine. The CIA was also involved in a 2024 prisoner swap deal with Russia that saw the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, as well as former US marine Paul Whelan and Russian-American journalist Alsu Kurmasheva. The US has had strained relations with Russia since it launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Russia has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions. Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit the country during President Donald Trump's second term. Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled. Additional reporting by Washington correspondent Daniel Bush and BBC Verify

item.title: Mass arrests in global crackdown on West African cyber-crime networks
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5xdnxppl4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Mass arrests in global crackdown on West African cyber-crime networks - Published Fifty-eight people linked to organised West African cyber-crime groups have been arrested in an operation across 22 countries and six continents. Dubbed "Operation Jackal IV", it was co-ordinated by the global policing agency Interpol, targeting those behind romance and investment scams. It also identified 263 suspects. Interpol said it was a response to the escalating global threat posed by these criminal networks - such as the feared Nigerian Black Axe group - believed to be behind a "significant share" of cyber-enabled financial fraud. The operation also allowed analysis of emerging trends such as how these groups use sextortion to target minors, with victims as young as 14. - The ultra-violent cult that became a global mafia - Published13 December 2021 Operation Jackal IV - which took place between November 2025 and June 2026 - investigated how the groups laundered money and how financial fraud cyber crimes, such as cryptocurrency and email compromise fraud, were conducted. Scams often targeted "retirees in English-speaking countries", Interpol said. "By following illicit financial flows across borders, we are attacking the very lifeblood of organised crime and making it increasingly difficult for criminal networks to profit from their activities," Tomonobu Kaya, director of Interpol's financial crime centre, said in a statement. "Operation Jackal IV demonstrates the power of international co-operation." During the operation, Interpol helped with cross-border co-ordination and intelligence sharing. It also provided support and specialised training for money-laundering investigations with the participating countries. Interpol said many aspects of Jackal IV remained under investigation but preliminary outcomes included arrests in Argentina, Italy, Romania and South Africa. In South Africa, seven sites linked to a syndicate involved in romance and investment scams were raided. The policing agency was on scene in Johannesburg to support local authorities during the raids. South African police made 39 arrests, seized $2.67m (£1.96m) and blocked 257 bank accounts. As well as cyber-enabled fraud, the West African networks also participated in other serious and violent crimes, Interpol said. Operation Jackal IV is one of multiple "Jackal" police operations that have taken place since 2022. In 2024, Jackal III led to the arrests of 300 people linked to Black Axe and other affiliated groups. Black Axe is a shadowy criminal network with trafficking, prostitution and killing operations around the world. Nigeria is its main recruitment ground and many of its members are university educated and inducted during their schooling. - Dead in 6 hours: How Nigerian sextortion scammers targeted my son - Published9 June 2024 - Notorious Instagram influencer jailed for fraud - Published8 November 2022 - Why Nigerian cyber fraudsters are 'role models' - Published23 September 2019 Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. item.title: Brain disease in dead NFL players 'higher than previously shown'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/american-football/articles/cew9l95kyp0o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Brain disease in dead NFL players 'higher than previously shown' - Published As many as 97.7% of NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 could have had brain disease related to repeated blows to the head, a new study says. Researchers looked at 878 former players who died during that period, with 235 having donated their brains to research. Of those, 215 were found to have chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease which can only be diagnosed after death. The study, published in the British Medical Journal, external, also found dementia was common among brain donors. "We and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population," said the report's lead author Daniel Daneshvar, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School. "These findings indicate that NFL players have a higher prevalence of CTE at death than has been previously shown in multiple community based studies." Researchers calculated a "conservative minimum" of CTE prevalence among those who died in the six-year period to be 24.5% - rising to a "maximum" 97.7%. They have urged the NFL to take prevention measures to reduce repetitive head impacts across all levels of the sport. - NFL admits football-brain disease link - Published15 March 2016 - New research finds link between head impacts & CTE - Published27 July 2022 "The bulk of the head impacts that these former NFL players experienced didn't occur at the NFL level," Danshvar said. "They occurred at the collegiate level and at the high school level and in many cases the youth level. And all of those cumulative hits to the head added up to result in an increased risk." An NFL spokesperson said: "The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts. "The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust - and expanding - set of resources to enhance their physical and mental well being. "We encourage former players to utilise these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health." CTE among American football players has been a growing issue in recent years. A 2011 Collective Bargaining Agreement for the NFL limited the number of contact practices. Following a long-running class action, in 2016 the NFL agreed a $1bn (£700m) settlement with more than 5,000 former players. Related topics - Published8 June

item.title: Tornado tears through French village, leaving dozens hurt and homes ravaged
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0m3npvpgdno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Tornado tears through French village, leaving dozens hurt and homes ravaged - Published A tornado has torn through the village of Pomas in south-west France, injuring 39 people and damaging hundreds of homes. Authorities said 15 people were taken to hospital and two were in a critical condition. One man said his pregnant wife was injured after their house collapsed on her. More than 120 emergency workers were deployed to the village south of Carcassonne after winds reaching 117km/h (73mph) tore roofs off houses and damaged an estimated 300 homes on Monday. "Half the village has been destroyed," said one resident called Pierre, who described the tornado as swirling like a "huge red and yellow chimney". "There's a huge castle and a third of it is has collapsed - even though these are stones that have stood for 1,000 years," Pierre told Ici Occitanie. The third stage of the Vuelta a España cycle race, which was taking place in the Aude area of south-western France, had to be cancelled when a hail storm forced the riders to take shelter about 15km from the finish line. The extreme weather has left about 2,800 homes across 10 villages without electricity, according to officials. Local sub-prefect Emmanuelle Plantier-Lemarchand told French radio that she was not aware of anyone missing. She lowered the number of victims from 41 to 39, and said 15 of them had been treated in hospital. "I heard this massive noise... then I saw everything flying around in the air and my roof collapsed over my head," shocked resident Chantal told French radio. "I've got no house left, that's for sure... I was really scared. I thought that's it, this my final hour." French authorities had issued an orange alert for thunderstorms in large parts of the country's south-west, which have already been hit by power outages and transport disruptions. Eyewitness footage from the region captured the swirling vortex of the tornado looming in the horizon above houses and trees. Images from the small village of Pomas, which was the hardest hit, showed uprooted trees, damaged cars and rubble from destroyed homes. Meanwhile there were flight delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and north of Paris to the north, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot. On average, France experiences several dozen tornadoes per year, according to the country's national weather service Météo-France. It comes after Europe's summer of unprecedented heatwaves and wildfires, with France's south-west region among the worst affected with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in one of the largest forest fires since World War Two. item.title: European rights court orders Turkey to free imprisoned businessman
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn5drvyg92no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
European rights court orders Turkey to free imprisoned businessman - Published The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ordered Turkey to immediately release Osman Kavala, an activist and philanthropist who has been detained in prison for almost a decade. Kavala was sentenced to life behind bars in 2022 for charges related to nationwide protests in 2013 and a failed coup attempt three years later. Since his initial arrest and detention in 2017, rights groups and Kavala himself have maintained that the charges against him are politically motivated. The ECHR on Tuesday ruled that his continued detention was unlawful and that his rights to a fair trial, freedom of expression and association had been violated. "The measures taken against the applicant... had been predominantly motivated by an ulterior purpose, namely, to punish him for his role in the Gezi Park demonstrations and for expressing his opinions as a human rights defender, and to silence him," the court said in its ruling, external. The court also found that Kavala's aggravated life sentence amounted to "inhuman and degrading treatment". Rights advocates and opposition groups say President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government has increasingly weaponised the judiciary to target critics and rivals. The court said Kavala's case had exposed a "systemic problem" in Turkey of the "detention and prosecution of political opponents, human rights defenders and journalists", adding that there were "structural shortcomings which affected the guarantees of independence and impartiality of the judiciary". The Turkish government has insisted the country's courts are independent. - Turkish activist sentenced to life in prison - Published26 April 2022 - The case that set Turkey on collision course with the West - Published25 November 2021 Kavala, 68, became a symbol of a government crackdown on civil society in Turkey following his arrest in October 2017. He and others were accused of orchestrating and financing anti-government protests in 2013, which started in Istanbul's Gezi park before spreading across Turkey. The demonstrations posed the first serious challenge to the rule of Erdogan, who was Turkey's dominant prime minister at the time and became its directly elected president the following year. Human rights group Amnesty International says prosecutors falsely alleged that the Gezi park protests were an attempt to overthrow the government. In 2019, the ECHR demanded Kavala's immediate release, describing his detention as arbitrary and politically motivated. Turkey did not implement the ruling. He was initially acquitted in February 2020 but within hours was rearrested on new charges of being part of a failed military coup in 2016. His acquittal over the Gezi Park protests was overturned in January 2021, and he was sentenced to life in prison in April 2022 - a conviction now declared "null and void" by the ECHR. Reacting to the latest ECHR ruling, Amnesty International's Eve Geddie said: "This obstruction of justice must end. Turkey's authorities, including judicial and prosecutorial, must act to free Osman Kavala immediately and unconditionally." Kavala was born in Paris and educated in the UK. Before being thrust to prominence, he ran a cultural centre. Erdogan has previously accused Kavala of being an agent of the Hungarian-born US billionaire George Soros. Turkey has refused to comply with the two previous ECHR rulings on Kavala's case, and it is not clear whether Ankara will implement the court's third binding ruling. The case remains one of the most serious recent flashpoints between Ankara and Strasbourg. The Council of Europe oversees how its 46 member states execute ECHR rulings. It has the power to freeze a country's membership or suspend its voting rights if it is found to have seriously violated the rule of law. Even though Turkey has failed to comply with several key ECHR decisions, it remains a founding member, engages with the system and has not broken ties. A meeting of the Committee of Ministers in mid-September is likely to prioritise the Kavala case, but it remains to be seen whether it will debate harsh punitive measures.

item.title: Nigeria's president orders manhunt after kidnappers upload victim video
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0rewkerdpyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Nigeria's president orders manhunt after kidnappers upload victim video - Published Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has ordered a manhunt for armed kidnappers who launched deadly attacks on four villages in a remote part of Niger state last Friday. Local residents told the BBC several mosques were simultaneously targeted during prayers. A local youth leader says as many as 500 people may have been abducted, though this has not been verified. The president's orders came after the kidnappers posted a video on social media of what they said were those abducted last week sitting in a forest. The authorities had previously suspected the attackers were bandits - criminal gangs involved in kidnapping and looting for ransom across parts of Nigeria. No ransom demands have been reported. - The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria - Published28 November 2025 The gunmen, reportedly dressed in military-style clothing, attacked the villages of Dekara, Gidan Zana, Sabon Gida and Masaka. Police spokesman Wasiu Abiodun told the BBC that more than 40 people were killed, but the exact number of deaths had not been confirmed. Looking at the footage released on social media, the local youth leader, who asked not to be named, said he recognised several individuals from his community. "I was able to identify many people. There is an elderly man in the video who is like a grandfather to us," he said. "He lives in Gidan Zana village." He said families who had spotted relatives in the video were relieved to know they were still alive. "At least they know where their loved ones are and hope they may be rescued, unlike those who still have no information about missing relatives," he added. A local blogger familiar with the area told the BBC that many residents had fled their homes, seeking refuge in neighbouring states or across the border in Benin. Some survivors are receiving hospital treatment, including people with serious injuries. A local official also told the BBC that the attackers planted improvised explosive devices in parts of the affected communities as they led abductees into the forest. He said a teenage boy was killed when an explosive detonated as he tried to escape. In a statement issued by presidential spokesman Bayo Onanuga, Tinubu condemned the killings and abductions and vowed that those responsible would be brought to justice. "Those who carried out this cowardly attack on defenceless Nigerians are enemies of peace and enemies of humanity, who will not go scot-free," the statement said. The president also expressed his condolences to the families of those killed. The attack is the latest sign of worsening insecurity in the Borgu area, which borders Kebbi and Kwara states as well as neighbouring Benin. Earlier this month, police said 145 people had been rescued after being abducted from four other villages in the area. Local officials have also raised concerns about the growing presence of jihadist groups operating in parts of north-western Nigeria and along the border region, saying some fighters have recently entered communities and imposed religious restrictions on residents. item.title: Lockerbie bombing trial postponed days before it was due to start
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq63rmj1zl1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Lockerbie bombing trial postponed days before it was due to start - Published The trial of a Libyan man over the Lockerbie bombing has been postponed for a third time, after new evidence on the 37-year-old case came to light three days ago. Jury selection was due to get under way in Washington DC on Wednesday but the BBC understands a new start date has been set for January next year. Lawyers acting for Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi said "newly discovered evidence" previously unknown to the defence and prosecutors from the US government emerged on Friday 21 August. Al-Marimi has denied building the bomb that destroyed Pan Am Flight 103 on 21 December 1988, killing 270 people. His lawyers told the court: "Constitutional and ethical obligations require the defence to investigate this development." They said they met Al-Marimi on Sunday and he agreed that they should ask for the postponement. The trial judge, Dabney Friedrich, has agreed that the start date should be set aside, underlining the potential importance of the new evidence. She would have been extremely reluctant to allow an 11th hour postponement after months of preparation and marathon pre-trial legal battles. For the relatives of those who died and Al-Marimi himself, this latest delay means a verdict might not come until next spring. It is yet another stunning development in a saga that has witnessed countless twists and turns over nearly four decades. Pan Am 103 was flying from Heathrow to New York when the bomb exploded in its forward hold, breaking the plane apart at 31,000 feet. All 259 passengers and crew on board were killed. Another 11 people died in Lockerbie when the wreckage fell on their homes. Of the victims, 190 were American and 43 from the UK. Nearly four decades later, the bombing remains the worst terror attack and mass murder in British history. Al-Marimi has been in US custody since 2022 and was originally due to stand trial in May 2025. That date was set aside following a joint request from the prosecution and defence, who cited the complexity of the case and Al-Marimi's ill health. The trial was pencilled in for April this year but was called off again, after the defence asked for more time to prepare. The Lockerbie bombing has been the subject of a joint Scottish-US investigation since December 1988. Prosecutors from the Crown Office and detectives from Police Scotland were due to travel to Washington to attend the case, and Scottish witnesses were expected to be among the first to give evidence at the trial. Laura Buchan, head of the Lockerbie investigation team at the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service said: "I recognise that this adjournment will be disappointing for the families and for those who have followed this case over many years. "As the matter remains before the court, it would not be appropriate to comment on the reasons for the adjournment. "Although these proceedings are being led by the United States authorities, Scottish prosecutors and police officers remain fully committed to supporting the pursuit of justice." Campaigner Kara Weipz, who is president of the Victims of Pan Am Flight 103 group, said she was "floored" when she received the news that the trial had been postponed. She told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme that she would pray that older relatives of victims would "remain healthy" so they can see the trial eventually take place. She said: "It's always been my goal for as many family members to be able to witness this trial as possible and to gain more of the truth. "If that's what this evidence brings, that's what the families have been fighting for for almost four decades - we want the truth, we want to know what happened - and if that's what this brings then this time will be worth it." Dr Jim Swire, who has campaigned for justice since his daughter, Flora, was killed in the bombing, said he believed the delay in the trial could be beneficial if it meant more care would be taken over evidence. He said: "For many years, we've been after only one thing, and that is the truth. "If each delay allows the court to assemble more of the true evidence, I am all in favour of it. "The judge seems to have stuck her oar in and insisted on further care being taken about the assembly of evidence, and if so, that is good news." A grandfather in his 70s, Al-Marimi has been accused of carrying out the attack along with two Libyans who faced a Scottish court in May 2000. Three judges heard the case at Camp Zeist, a former US air force base in the Netherlands. After eight months, they ruled the atrocity was an act of state sponsored terrorism carried out by members of the Libyan intelligence service. Intrigue: Lockerbie On 21 December 1988, a plane explodes over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people. Almost four decades on, there's fresh evidence. Who was really behind the bombing? The judges convicted one of the Libyans, Abdulbasset Al-Megrahi, of mass murder and jailed him for life. He died from cancer in 2012, after being freed on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government. The Scottish Criminal Cases Review Commission twice referred Megrahi's case to the appeal court but the conviction was upheld. The second Libyan, Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah was acquitted and returned home to a hero's welcome in Tripoli. The US government says Al-Marimi admitted bombing the plane along with Megrahi and Fhimah when he was questioned in a Libyan detention facility in 2012. The alleged confession was handed to Scottish investigators in 2017 and is now central to the prosecution case. Al-Marimi has claimed the confession is false and was made under duress, but judge Friedrich ruled it can be admitted as evidence at the trial. - Lockerbie: Remembering the victims of Flight 103 - Published2 June 2025 - Lockerbie bombing: The ultimate detective story? - Published15 December 2023 Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Swedish military seeks to take over Russian-owned estate near naval base - Published Sweden's armed forces have asked the government to expropriate a Russia-owned property near a naval base on security grounds. The military requested the seizure of the beach plot near Muskö base in Stockholm archipelago, citing "the threat from Russian drones and the ownership situation of the property". Swedish reports say a businessman with links to the Russian state, has been building a luxury house on Muskö island – although his wife, who holds both Russian and Swedish citizenship, is the registered owner. Two years ago, Sweden ended two centuries of military non-alignment and joined Nato because of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In its statement, the military said the location had "unique conditions for strengthening the defence of Muskö Naval Base, particularly against drones". The development of Russian drone warfare has "changed the threat landscape for Sweden", the military added. Public broadcaster SVT said the property has been "a thorn in the armed forces' side". Defence Minister Pål Jonson said the country needed to "make sure there's no risk of anyone gaining visibility into the site or any kind of tactical edge", Sweden's TV4 reported. The armed forces' statement quoted Chief of the Defence Staff Carl-Johan Edström as saying that Sweden was "facing the most serious security situation since the end of World War Two". It is unclear whether the Russian businessman is currently living in Sweden. His wife is reported to have owned the property since 2017.

item.title: Two unvaccinated people die of measles in Pennsylvania
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yednen30go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Two unvaccinated people die of measles in Pennsylvania - Published Two people who were not vaccinated against measles have died of the virus in Pennsylvania, health officials said. The state has seen 393 cases of the highly contagious virus this year, as infections across the US have hit the highest point in 35 years. Eighty-five percent of kindergarten-age students in Lancaster County, where the recent deaths occurred, are vaccinated against measles - well below the 95% rate needed for herd immunity to limit the spread and protect immunocompromised people. Last year, two unvaccinated children in Texas died from a measles outbreak that infected over 1,000 people, primarily children. "This is a serious and a growing problem across our country and in our commonwealth," Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said in a news conference on Tuesday. "This illness and death from measles is completely preventable." He added that the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) vaccine was the best tool to protect against illness and death. Officials said they would not share any additional information on the identities of those who died, including if they were children, who have face a higher risk of death and complications from measles. The US has seen 2,777 confirmed cases of measles in 2026, just seven months into the year, up from last year's high of 2,289. The rising number of cases comes as vaccine hesitancy in the US has increased in recent years, leading to lower immunisation rates. The US recommends two shots to children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness. Earlier this month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that calls for fewer childhood vaccinations and recommends splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate shots. Public health experts worry the order will cause confusion about an already safe and effective vaccine and prove costly. The executive order came after Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr took a number of steps to remake US vaccine policies over the past year, including the childhood vaccination schedule. Many of the changes were blocked by a federal judge earlier this year. A vaccine skeptic, Kennedy has shared mixed messaging on the MMR vaccine, at times endorsing it and other times sharing unproven claims about its safety. Speaking on Tuesday, Shapiro said he spoke with Kennedy over the phone that morning and that he had offered to send staff from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Shapiro said he was "very blunt" with Kennedy about vaccinations. "I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that's coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America ... that there's real life consequences to spreading misinformation," Shapiro said. The US is on track to lose its status of having eliminated measles, which will be determined by a panel in November. Canada lost its status last year.

item.title: French tourist dies in Death Valley after car gets stuck in mud
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyl81jlzr2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
French tourist dies in Death Valley after car gets stuck in mud - Published A French tourist has died in California's Death Valley after becoming stranded on the side of the road during 46.6C (116F) heat. Police found 68-year-old Pierre Michel Formosa recently following a brief search, with the National Park service saying he died while trying to seek help in the blistering heat when his car got stuck in mud. "This is a heartbreaking reminder of how quickly conditions here can turn dangerous," Death Valley National Park Superintendent Mike Reynolds said in a statement. Soaring temperatures across the United States have caused millions of people to sweat through record heatwaves, leading to dozens of heat-related deaths. Formosa was driving through Death Valley with his French travelling companion last Monday when their vehicle became stuck in mud on West Side Road. The pair sought help by walking across the salt flats, before severe heat prevented the 68-year-old from continuing after 1.3 miles, according to the Death Valley National Park. The travelling companion managed to hail down a nearby driver, before rangers and police found Formosa later that afternoon where he was pronounced dead. "Death Valley is an extraordinary place, but its heat, distances, and remoteness can be dangerous, regardless of experience," Reynolds said. "We're grateful to everyone who took part in the search, and our thoughts are with his loved ones." Coroners would determine the cause and manner of his death, the national park said. An extreme heat warning is currently in effect across Death Valley, which brands itself as the "hottest place on Earth", according to its official website, having recorded a global high of 57C (134F) in 1913. Forecasters at the National Weather Service expected Southern California would experience its "hottest week of summer so far", the bureau said in a recent statement. Record heatwaves have endangered tourists visiting US landmarks throughout the summer. At least four hikers died in June while trekking through the Grand Canyon, state authorities reported in Arizona.

item.title: US firefighters say major blaze near Reno about a quarter contained
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gqlp0yzyjo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US firefighters say major blaze near Reno about a quarter contained - Published US fire crews have reported progress in their efforts to tackle a large wildfire menacing the city of Reno, Nevada - saying the blaze is about a quarter contained. The Hawk Fire, which began on Saturday, had spread over 15,000 acres by Monday, firefighters said. Evacuation orders remain in place for 23,000 people, though other residents have now been allowed to return to their homes. Tens of thousands of other residents have been told to be ready to leave at any moment. Officials are concerned that gusts of wind could drive the flames towards more homes. Unfavourable weather conditions are forecast for the next two days, meaning the fire could continue to burn during that timeframe. No deaths have been reported, though seven people have been injured. The fire, which was first reported on Saturday morning, spread in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains near Reno due to those same windy and unpredictable weather conditions. The immediate "go now" evacuation zone and wider "get set" area - where people are being warned to prepare to evacuate - do not extend to the centre of Reno, but they do affect large urban areas and part of a highway. Large air tankers and helicopters have been flying over the affected area dropping water and fire retardants. In their update on Monday afternoon, fire officials said the blaze had been at least 27% contained. Chief Richard Edwards, of the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District, said those injured were four civilians and three firefighters, who suffered minor burns. Edwards added that 32 homes had been destroyed and six damaged, and that those numbers were expected to increase. Shelters have been set up in the area to take in displaced residents. While firefighters have made progress, more than two-thirds of the fire's perimeter remains uncontained. The fire is thought to have been caused by humans. Edwards added on Monday that investigators did not yet know if the blaze was set intentionally. Scientists say that human-induced climate change makes the warm, dry conditions more likely that assist the rapid spread of wildfires. Reno's average temperature has gone up by over 4C since the 1970s, faster than any other big US city, according to Climate Central. Nevada's Governor Joe Lombardo earlier declared a state of emergency in surrounding Washoe County, and ordered the National Guard to join firefighting and law enforcement efforts. "This is an active and rapidly evolving situation and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," he said on Saturday. Firefighters from Australia and New Zealand have so far taken part in the containment effort – as well as crews from 15 US states. The University of Nevada in Reno - which has its main campus in the city close to the "get set" warning area - previously said regular campus operations would continue but that it was monitoring the situation. But one student, James Wolfgang Perez, said some teaching staff had independently decided to cancel their classes. The sight of the fire spreading in the direction of the campus on Saturday had been "apocalyptic", he told the BBC. Justin Davis, 29, lives on Peavine Mountain, close to Reno, and similarly watched as the fire spread towards his home on Saturday and destroyed four of his vehicles. He told the BBC he had previously bought a water truck in case a wildfire like this occurred and had used it to save his home. "We turned on the water truck and just started spraying down the things we wanted to save," he said. The blaze has been been named the Hawk Fire because it was first reported near the Hawk Meadow Trail, to the west of Reno. Reno, in western Nevada, is located close to the state boundary with California and has a population of around 280,000 people. Wildfires are common in south-western US states, including Nevada, and are becoming more severe, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Many of these fires develop in rural and less populated areas, with only a few encroaching on population centres. Are you in the area? If it is safe to do so, share your story. item.title: Kit Harington replaces Nicholas Hoult in HBO's Harry Potter series

========================================
Kit Harington replaces Nicholas Hoult in HBO's Harry Potter series - Published Kit Harington is joining the highly anticipated Harry Potter TV series as the wizarding world's celebrity-turned-Hogwarts instructor Gilderoy Lockhart. X-Men star Nicholas Hoult was originally cast in the second series earlier this month but has now left due to scheduling issues, according to HBO. Best known for playing Jon Snow in Game of Thrones, Harington also appears in BBC and HBO financial drama Industry. The star previously voiced Lockhart in an audio version of Harry Potter. "I'm a huge Potter fan. I've got to be honest, he's one of my favourite characters," Harington told Collider, external. "So, to be offered to play him is a real dream. I've had a taste of him [in the audiobook] and felt my way around him. He's just a wonderful creation." Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone is due to premiere this Christmas on HBO Max. Season two will adapt the second book in the series by JK Rowling, The Chamber of Secrets, which chronicles Potter's second year at the magical school. "Before we begin year two at Hogwarts, there has been a slight change due to schedule: Kit Harington will be stepping into the role of Gilderoy Lockhart," an HBO statement said, external. The new series adaptation of the best-selling books stars newcomer Dominic McLaughlin as the boy wizard, Alastair Stout as his best friend Ron Weasley and Arabella Stanton as the young witch Hermione Granger. Oscar-nominated actor Jon Lithgow has been cast as Hogwarts headmaster Albus Dumbledore and Nick Frost will play gamekeeper Rubeus Hagrid. The show could reunite Harington, who has said he is a lifelong fan of the books, with director and producer Mark Mylod, who worked on Game of Thrones and is directing some Harry Potter episodes. Mylod is an executive producer on the new series along with author JK Rowling. Lockhart was portrayed in the Harry Potter films by Kenneth Branagh, and is a key character in Rowling's second book in the hugely successful book series. The vain wizard, who authored several books on his purported encounters with dark creatures, serves as Hogwarts' latest professor for the defence against the dark arts and fancies himself as a mentor to Harry in his second year. Hoult, along with other cast members, has faced some backlash for his decision to join the show from those who are opposed to Rowling's views on gender identity and trans rights. Representatives for Harington and Hoult did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The HBO series is expected to take 10 years to complete, as producers plan multiple seasons covering each of Rowling's seven books, which the eight blockbuster films were originally based on. - Published12 August - Published26 February 2025 - Published25 March

item.title: NZ religious sect leader jailed over death of Chinese follower
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3d79z4z953o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
NZ religious sect leader jailed over death of Chinese follower - Published A New Zealand court has jailed a religious sect leader over the death of an elderly follower who had travelled from China to live with his family. Kaixiao Liu was found guilty of manslaughter and kidnapping, and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison. The body of 70-year-old Shulai Wang had been found wrapped in rice bags near Auckland's Gulf Harbour in March 2024, sparking a major homicide investigation which eventually led to Liu. Liu, a musician who previously appeared in a talent show in China, had denied the charges. He also denied he is a cult leader and said he only attracted followers through his music. During the trial the court heard that Wang had travelled from Hainan island in China to New Zealand in August 2023. She moved in with Liu and his family at their house, which Liu had called "the Ark", along with several other female followers. Prosecutors said that the women acted in "servitude" to Liu and his family, and their lives were tightly controlled by Liu, where they referred to him as "Lord" or "Master". Wang reportedly spent her days taking care of Liu's children, studying scripture, and planting vegetables. The court heard that Wang had struggled to comply with the strict rules, possibly due to her old age, and was frequently disciplined. In March 2024, Wang tried to escape but was caught and restrained. She died later that day, the court heard. The court heard that Liu, his family, and his followers dumped Wang's body near a marina at Gulf Harbour. Liu had taken his children along for the trip "as camouflage". The body was found by a fisherman days later. Police eventually traced the rice bags used to wrap Wang's body to Liu, who had made unusually large purchases of that brand of rice. Besides Liu, his wife, Lanyue Xiao, was sentenced to nearly eight years in jail for kidnapping and manslaughter, amongst other charges. His mother, Xiuyun Li and father, Jingui Liu, had earlier been convicted of kidnapping and misconduct to human remains and are due to be sentenced later this year. On Tuesday's sentencing, Liu's lawyer asked for leniency arguing that his client feels remorse and "is not a cult leader, nor requires people to follow his cult", according to Radio New Zealand. New Zealand media outlets reported that Liu had attended a military-based university in China. In 2011, he was a contestant for China's Got Talent - clips posted online showed him singing onstage blindfolded. Sometime in 2017, he moved to New Zealand along with Xiao, and the couple became permanent residents. Liu attracted followers on Chinese social media where he posted religious discussions, video diaries, and clips of himself singing. He also set up a project called Universal Choir that produced cosmic-themed orchestral music. During the trial a police officer who interviewed one of Liu's female followers gave testimony. He said in court that the woman told him she "met the people over the internet through a song website, and she referred to the occupants of the house as friends". During the sentencing, Justice Mathew Downs said Liu had shown "callous indifference" towards Wang. "Because of you, Ms Wang died a lonely, frightening death. You display no remorse whatsoever. You should feel shame."

item.title: US removes Syria from list of state sponsors of terrorism
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c33knmyl0y5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US removes Syria from list of state sponsors of terrorism - Published The US has removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism after 47 years, lifting what it said was the "final major barriers" for private sector investment in the country and its reintegration into the global economy. US Secretary Of State Marco Rubio said the move was in recognition of the Syrian government's positive actions to fully distance itself from acts of international terrorism. The Trump administration has embraced Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former militant who once had an American bounty on his head as the leader of an al-Qaeda off-shoot. His Islamist group, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), was also removed from the US list of global terrorist organisations. HTS, formerly known as al-Nusra Front, was al-Qaeda's affiliate in Syria until Sharaa severed ties with the jihadist network in 2016. In late 2024, HTS led the rebel offensive that overthrew former president Bashar al-Assad and it dominates Sharaa's transitional administration. The US hopes to bring Syria into its orbit rather than that of Russia or China. But the risks remain significant, with Syria still far from secure and lacking representative government. It is also at the centre of growing tensions between its neighbours Israel and Turkey. Rubio said Monday's move, which had been initially flagged in July, would give the Syrians "a path to prosperity". US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "Today's action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability." Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani greeted the news as a "historic step", according to state-run news agency SANA. "We will continue working to remove the effects of isolation and create an environment based on transparency, mutual interests and respect," he said. Last year, the US also revoked the designation of HTS as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation and removed Sharaa from its list of Specially Designated Global Terrorists. Syria's removal from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism - where it had been since 1979 - leaves just three remaining: Cuba, North Korea and Iran. The listing carries financial sanctions, restrictions on US foreign aid and defence exports and sales and can also penalise people and other countries that trade with the sanctioned state. item.title: Sonya Massey's killer Sean Grayson dies in US prison
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgrvj28wrxgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Sonya Massey's killer Sean Grayson dies in US prison - Published Sean Grayson, the white US police officer convicted of murdering a black woman, Sonya Massey, during an incident at her home in 2024, has died in prison at age 32. Grayson shot dead Massey, 36, during an exchange that took place after she reported a suspected intruder at her residence in Illinois. The killing reignited the debate about police brutality in the US. Grayson said he fired because he thought Massey was about to throw a pot of boiling water on him. He was last year found guilty of second-degree murder. The former police officer was undergoing treatment for colon cancer. His lawyer Daniel Fultz confirmed to the BBC that Grayson had died on Sunday, but did not disclose the cause. The Illinois Department of Corrections said it could only confirm that Grayson had died at a facility outside the state, and likewise did not provide a cause. Lawyers for Massey's family said: "Grayson's death in custody from cancer does not bring Sonya back." "We wish his family prayers of peace, as we do for all who grieve a loved one. Sonya's family knows that pain all too well and will grieve her loss the rest of their days," the lawyers said, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. Protests took place across the US in the aftermath of Massey's death, and then-President Joe Biden declared that the late woman "should be alive today". - Ex-officer guilty of murder of Sonya Massey after she reported suspected intruder - Published29 October 2025 The incident took place in the early hours over Independence Day weekend in July 2024. Massey called police to her home in Springfield, 200 miles (320km) south of Chicago, to report that she believed someone had broken in to her property. Police bodycam footage of the incident showed the chaotic sequence of events. The shooting happened after an exchange of words about a pot on Massey's stove. Massey and Grayson appeared to laugh over her pot of "steaming hot water", before Massey twice said: "I rebuke you in the name of Jesus." "You better [expletive] not or I swear to God I'll [expletive] shoot you in your [expletive] face," Grayson said. He then drew his pistol as he shouted for her to drop the pot. "OK, I'm sorry," Massey was heard saying before she ducked. Grayson fired three shots, striking her in the face. Grayson, who was subsequently sacked from his job, was charged with first-degree murder, but the jury was allowed to convict him of the lesser charge of second-degree murder. He was sentenced to 20 years in prison. In recent months, he applied for release on medical grounds, but was unsuccessful. He had been diagnosed with cancer in 2023.

King of Norway's health has worsened, palace says - Published King Harald V of Norway's health has worsened, the palace has said, as he remains in hospital receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his bloodstream. The monarch has responded to treatment despite the deterioration in his condition, according to the palace, but he will remain at Oslo University Hospital, Rikshospitalet, and on leave from royal duties until further notice. The 89-year-old, who has been on the throne since 1991, was admitted to hospital and put on sick leave a week ago. His son, Crown Prince Haakon, 53, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave. King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia. It causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. In April 2024, Norway's royal household said that King Harald would make a "permanent reduction" to his public engagements "out of consideration for his age". That year, the king had been fitted with a pacemaker after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia. The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026. Crown Prince Haakon's wife, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018. The transplant came two days after Mette-Marit's son Marius Borg Høiby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges and his lawyers said he would appeal the sentence. Høiby, 29, was four when his mother married Crown Prince Haakon and is not himself a royal figure. Also earlier in the year, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. She later apologised to Norway's king and queen for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.
